name: Cohesion: reference, substitution, ellipsis
subtitle: A good text holds together. Reference words such as this and the latter point back to what you have already said. Substitution (one, do so, so) and ellipsis (leaving words out) avoid repetition, and linking adverbs such as however join sentences.
source: icanspeak English original English text (grammar-c1 run, 2026-10-29)

concept.exampleHtml: The council raised parking fees. This decision upset many drivers. However, the extra income is badly needed.

qa.html: Reference: it points back to one noun. This / that / these / those + a summary noun point back to a whole idea: The council closed the pool. This decision upset many families. Use this for the idea you have just said. Such also works: Such a decision is rarely popular. For two things named before, use the former (the first) and the latter (the second): Tom and Amira applied. The former got the job. These are formal and written.

Substitution: one / ones replace a countable noun (I like the red bag, not the blue one.). Do so replaces a verb phrase, in formal writing (Staff may leave early, but few do so.). So and not replace a whole clause after think, hope, believe, expect, suppose, be afraid: "Will it rain?" "I think so." / "I hope not." The same repeats a whole thing: I'll have the same.

Ellipsis means leaving out words that are clear from the context: Tom can swim, but I can't. (= can't swim) She wanted to go, but I didn't want to. The auxiliary stays, and to stays at the end. In short answers: "Who called?" "Mia."

Linking adverbs join a sentence to the one before: however, moreover, nevertheless, therefore, as a result, in contrast, on the other hand, meanwhile. They are not conjunctions. Use a full stop or a semicolon before them and a comma after: The test was hard. However, most students passed. The test was hard; however, most students passed. Each adverb has a job: addition, contrast, result, order.

Typical mistakes: ✗ The test was hard, however most students passed. → ✓ The test was hard. However, most students passed. (a comma alone cannot join two sentences) · ✗ Will it rain? I don't hope so. → ✓ I hope not. · ✗ She asked me to help, but I didn't want. → ✓ …but I didn't want to. (keep to after ellipsis)

concept.noteHtml: Adverb or conjunction? But, and, so join two clauses in one sentence: The hotel was cheap, but it was dirty. However and the others start a new sentence or follow a semicolon. They can also move: The hotel was dirty. It was cheap, however. Do not use one in every sentence; the text will sound mechanical. For although, despite see contrast and reason, and for whereas, given that see formal linkers. For one / ones after an adjective see the + adjective, one / ones. Be careful with it and this when two things are possible: Tom told Mia that he had failed. This surprised her. What surprised her: his failure or the telling? Then name it: This failure surprised her.

tables.caption: Reference words
head: Type
Words
Example
rows: The report was published in May. It caused a debate.
The council closed the pool. This decision upset many families.
Such a decision is rarely popular.
the first / the second of two
Tom and Amira applied. The former got the job.

tables.caption: Substitution and ellipsis
head: Device
What it replaces
Example
rows: I lost my umbrella, so I bought a new one.
Staff may leave early, but few do so.
She can drive, but I can't.

tables.caption: Linking adverbs by job
head: Job
Adverbs
Example
rows: The hotel is clean. Moreover, it is close to the beach.
however, nevertheless, in contrast, on the other hand
The test was hard. Nevertheless, most students passed.
The trains were cancelled. As a result, we took a taxi.
First, we compared prices. Finally, we booked.
for example, in other words, overall
Public transport is cheaper. For example, a monthly ticket costs less than petrol.

items: Full stop + comma: It was cheap. However, it broke.
Semicolon + comma: It was cheap; however, it broke.
In the middle: It broke, however, after a week.
✗ It was cheap, however it broke.
Prices rose. This rise worried people.
Prices rose. This trend is likely to continue.
If it is unclear what this refers to, name it.

listen.text: The council closed the pool. This decision upset many families.
listen.note: this + summary noun: This decision points back to the closing of the pool.

listen.text: I can't swim, but my sister can.
listen.note: Ellipsis: swim is left out after can. The auxiliary stays.

listen.text: The test was difficult. Nevertheless, most students passed.
listen.note: A linking adverb starts the new sentence and has a comma after it.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose what you hear. You can listen twice.

items.text: Will it rain tomorrow? I hope not.
Tom and Amira both applied. The latter got the job.
I lost my umbrella, so I bought a new one.
The tickets were expensive. Nevertheless, the show sold out.
She wanted to go, but I didn't want to.
Prices rose last year. As a result, many families spent less.

rounds.label: 1 · start the second sentence with the linking adverb
rounds.instruction: You hear two sentences and, in brackets, a linking adverb. Say both sentences and start the second one with the adverb.

example.prompt: The film was long. It was excellent. (however)
example.answer: The film was long. However, it was excellent.

items.prompt: The flat is small. It is cheap. (however)
items.answer: The flat is small. However, it is cheap.

items.prompt: The trains were cancelled. We arrived late. (as a result)
items.answer: The trains were cancelled. As a result, we arrived late.

items.prompt: The hotel is clean. It is close to the station. (moreover)
items.answer: The hotel is clean. Moreover, it is close to the station.

items.prompt: Tom likes jazz. Amira prefers rock. (in contrast)
items.answer: Tom likes jazz. In contrast, Amira prefers rock.

items.prompt: The test was hard. Most students passed. (nevertheless)
items.answer: The test was hard. Nevertheless, most students passed.

items.prompt: We booked online. We saved ten pounds. (therefore)
items.answer: We booked online. Therefore, we saved ten pounds.

rounds.label: 2 · ellipsis: leave the repeated words out
rounds.instruction: You hear two sentences. Join them with but, and leave out the repeated words. Keep the auxiliary.

example.prompt: Tom can swim. I can't swim.
example.answer: Tom can swim, but I can't.

items.prompt: Amira likes tea. Her sister doesn't like tea.
items.answer: Amira likes tea, but her sister doesn't.

items.prompt: I have been to Paris. My brother hasn't been to Paris.
items.answer: I have been to Paris, but my brother hasn't.

items.prompt: Liam wanted to go. I didn't want to go.
items.answer: Liam wanted to go, but I didn't want to.

items.prompt: Priya will come. Diego won't come.
items.answer: Priya will come, but Diego won't.

items.prompt: My neighbours have a car. We don't have a car.
items.answer: My neighbours have a car, but we don't.

items.prompt: Mei was invited. Olga wasn't invited.
items.answer: Mei was invited, but Olga wasn't.

exercises.title: What does the word refer to?
exercises.hint: The word in capitals points back to something. Choose what it stands for.

exercises.title: Which reference or substitute word fits?
exercises.hint: Think about what the word replaces: a noun, a verb phrase or a whole clause.

exercises.title: Which linking adverb fits?
exercises.hint: Decide the job: addition, contrast, result, order or example.

exercises.title: Which sentence can follow?
exercises.hint: Match each sentence with the one that picks it up with a pronoun or a summary word.

exercises.title: Gap text: A short report on cycling.
exercises.hint: Choose the word that refers back, replaces a word, or links the sentences.
